title: Chapter 54 — The Town-Ho’s Story
paragraphs: (As told at the Golden Inn.)
The Cape of Good Hope, and all the watery region around it, is much like some notable crossroads of a great highway, where you meet more travelers than in any other part.

It was not very long after speaking the Goney that another homeward-bound whaler, the Town-Ho, was encountered. She was manned almost entirely by Polynesians. In the short gam that followed, she gave us strong news of Moby Dick. To some, the general interest in the White Whale was now wildly heightened by a detail of the Town-Ho's story that seemed obscurely to involve with the whale a certain wondrous, inverted visitation of one of those so-called acts of divine judgment — a tale whose deeper meaning only a few of the Pequod's crew fully understood. To the rest of the ship's company, the story was simply about a fight between a mate and one of the crew, and that this man still remained on board, replacing the chief mate who had been killed. For all that, the Town-Ho's story was one to be told in darkness, and it is only now that I tell it in full. But let this be said at once: it was Steelkilt, the Town-Ho's crewman, who told the whole tale to Tashtego with a certain amount of secrecy on the forecastle of the Pequod, one dark night on the Japan cruising ground. But the very night Tashtego heard this amazing story, he raved in his sleep, and revealed so much of it that when he was awakened, he could not help himself. The secret was out. Nevertheless, so much of the story was withheld from the Pequod's officers that they knew nothing about Steelkilt's connection with the white whale, nor did they know how the terrible collision with that whale had been preceded by the darker conflict between two men on the Town-Ho. All they knew was the general tale of how the mate had been killed. This is the story Tashtego half-consciously told us. But for my humor's sake, I shall preserve the style in which I once narrated it at Lima, to a lounging circle of my Spanish friends on a saint's eve, smoking on the thick gold-tiled terrace of the Golden Inn.
The ancient whale-cry upon first sighting a whale from the masthead, still used by whalemen in hunting the famous Galapagos tortoise.

For my humor's sake, I shall preserve the style in which I once narrated it at Lima, to a lounging circle of my Spanish friends, one saint's eve, smoking upon the thick gold-tiled terrace of the Golden Inn. Of those fine gentlemen, the young Dons, Pedro and Sebastian, were on the closest terms with me, and hence the occasional questions they put, which are duly answered at the time.

"Some two years prior to my first learning the events which I am about to rehearse to you, gentlemen, the Town-Ho, Sperm Whaler of Nantucket, was cruising in your Pacific here, not very many days' sail eastward from the eaves of this good Golden Inn. She was somewhere to the northward of the Line. One morning upon handling the pumps, according to daily usage, it was observed that she made more water in her hold than common. They supposed a swordfish had stabbed her, gentlemen. But the captain, having some unusual reason for believing that rare good luck awaited him in those latitudes, and therefore being very averse to quit them, and the leak not being then considered at all dangerous, though, indeed, they could not find it after searching the hold as low down as was possible in rather heavy weather, the ship still continued her cruisings, the mariners working at the pumps at wide and easy intervals. But no good luck came; more days went by, and not only was the leak yet undiscovered, but it sensibly increased. So much so, that now taking some alarm, the captain, making all sail, stood away for the nearest harbor among the islands, there to have his hull hove out and repaired."

"Though a long passage lay ahead of her, yet if ordinary luck held, he did not at all fear that his ship would founder on the way, because his pumps were of the best. Being periodically relieved at them, his thirty-six men could easily keep the ship clear — never mind if the leak should double. In truth, since nearly the whole of this passage was attended by very good weather, the Town-Ho had all but certainly arrived at her destination in perfect safety, had it not been for the brutal overbearing of Radney, the mate, a native of Martha's Vineyard. And for the provoked vengeance of Steelkilt, a Lakeman and desperado from Buffalo."
"'Lakeman! — Buffalo! Pray, what is a Lakeman, and where is Buffalo?' said Don Sebastian, rising in his swinging grass hammock."

"On the eastern shore of our Lake Erie, Don; but — I crave your courtesy — may be, you shall soon hear further of all that. Now, gentlemen, in square-sail brigs and three-masted ships, well-nigh as large and stout as any that ever sailed out of your old Callao to far Manila, this Lakeman, in the land-locked heart of our America, had yet been nurtured by all those agrarian freebooting impressions popularly connected with the open ocean. For in their interflowing aggregate, those grand fresh-water seas of ours — Erie, and Ontario, and Huron, and Superior, and Michigan — possess an ocean-like expansiveness, with many of the ocean's noblest traits, with many of its rimmed varieties of races and of climes. They contain round archipelagoes of romantic isles, even as the Polynesian waters do; in large part, are shored by two great contrasting nations, as the Atlantic is; they furnish long maritime approaches to our numerous territorial colonies from the East, dotted all round their banks; here and there are frowned upon by batteries, and by the goat-like craggy guns of lofty Mackinaw; they have heard the fleet thunderings of naval victories; at intervals, they yield their beaches to wild barbarians, whose red painted faces flash from out their peltry wigwams; for leagues and leagues are flanked by ancient and unentered forests, where the gaunt pines stand like serried lines of kings in Gothic genealogies; those same woods harboring wild Afric beasts of prey, and silken creatures whose exported furs give robes to Tartar Emperors; they mirror the paved capitals of Buffalo and Cleveland, as well as Winnebago villages; they float alike the full-rigged merchant ship, the armed cruiser of the State, the steamer, and the beech canoe; they are swept by Borean and dismasting blasts as direful as any that lash the salted wave; they know what shipwrecks are, for out of sight of land, however inland, they have drowned full many a midnight ship with all its shrieking crew. Thus, gentlemen, though an inlander, Steelkilt was wild-ocean born, and wild-ocean nurtured; as much of an audacious mariner as any. And for Radney, though in his infancy he may have laid him down on the lone Nantucket beach, to nurse at his maternal sea; though in after life he had long followed our austere Atlantic and your contemplative Pacific — yet was he quite as vengeful and full of social quarrel as the backwoods seaman, fresh from the latitudes of buck-horn handled Bowie-knives. Yet was this Nantucketer a man with some good-hearted traits; and this Lakeman, a mariner, who though a sort of devil indeed, might yet by inflexible firmness, only tempered by that common decency of human recognition which is the meanest slave's right; thus treated, this Steelkilt had long been retained harmless and docile. At all events, he had proved so thus far; but Radney was doomed and made mad, and Steelkilt — but, gentlemen, you shall hear."

"It was not more than a day or two at most after setting course for her island harbor that the Town-Ho's leak seemed to be increasing again, but only enough to require an hour or more at the pumps each day. You should know that in a settled and civilized ocean like our Atlantic, for example, some captains think nothing of pumping their whole way across it. Though on a still, sleepy night, should the officer on watch happen to forget his duty in that respect, and the ship's pumping should cease, and the crew wake to the sound of the water washing over the cabin floor — the pumps going all day in such a case is not a thing that alarms anyone."

"Much this way it had been with the Town-Ho. So when her leak was found gaining once more, there was in truth some small concern among several of her company, especially Radney the mate. He ordered the upper sails hoisted and sheeted home anew, and every way spread to catch the breeze. Now this Radney, I suppose, was no more a coward, and no more inclined to any sort of nervous apprehension about the safety of his ship, than any other ordinary careful seaman. But coming from an island — Nantucket — where he had never met a hill bigger than a mole hill, where the horizon was the only boundary he could see, and where to his practical mind a leak in the ship was like a leak in his own body — his vigilance about the Town-Ho's leak was entirely natural. He was not half so afraid of the leak as he was of the reputation of being afraid. Still, the fact remained: Radney was afraid, and that fear drove everything he did next."

"Now, as you well know, it is not rare in this conventional world of ours — watery or otherwise — that when a person placed in command over his fellow-men finds one of them to be significantly his superior in general pride of manhood, right away he conceives an unconquerable dislike and bitterness toward that man. And if he has a chance, he will pull down and pulverize that subordinate's tower, and make a little heap of dust of it. Be that what it may, gentlemen, in Steelkilt, the Lakeman, the mate found his superior in general strength and fearlessness. And when the two were together, the contrast was a painful one for the mate."
"Spotting the mate drawing near as he was toiling at the pump with the rest, the Lakeman pretended not to notice him, and casually went on with his lighthearted joking."

"'Aye, aye, my merry lads, it's a lively leak this! Hold a cup, one of you, and let's have a taste. By the Lord, it's worth bottling! I tell you what, men, old Rad's investment must pay for it! He'd best cut away his part of the hull and tow it home. The fact is, boys, that sword-fish only started the job. He's come back again with a gang of ship-carpenters, saw-fish, and file-fish, and what not. And the whole gang is hard at work cutting and slashing at the bottom — making improvements, I suppose. If old Rad were here now, I'd tell him to jump overboard and scatter them. They're playing the devil with his property, I can tell you. But that's his lookout, not mine. I'm not paid to guard his things. Let him look after his own planks.'"
"'Damn your eyes! What's that pump stopping for?' roared Radney, pretending not to have heard the sailors' talk. 'Thunder away at it!'"

"'Aye, aye, sir,' said Steelkilt, merry as a cricket. 'Lively, boys, lively, now!' And with that the pump clanged like fifty fire-engines. The men tossed their hats off to it, and before long that peculiar gasping of the lungs was heard that marks the fullest strain of life's utmost energies."

"Leaving the pump at last, with the rest of his gang, the Lakeman went forward all panting and sat himself down on the windlass — his face fiery red, his eyes bloodshot, wiping the heavy sweat from his brow. Now what possessing devil it was, gentlemen, that drove Radney to bother such a man in that physically exhausted state, I don't know. But so it happened. Striding intolerably along the deck, the mate commanded him to get a broom and sweep down the decks, and also a shovel, and remove some offensive material left by the cattle on board."

"Now, gentlemen, sweeping a ship's deck at sea is a piece of housework which in all conditions but raging gales is regularly done every evening. It has been known to be done in the case of ships actually sinking at the time. Such, gentlemen, is the rigidity of sea customs and the instinctive love of neatness in seamen — some of whom would not willingly drown without first washing their faces. But in all ships this broom work is assigned to the boys of the crew. Besides, it was not the custom of the Town-Ho for her sailors to clean up after her cattle — that task belonged to the boys. And by boys, I do not mean children but simply the least experienced of the crew."

"But there was more than this: the order about the shovel was almost as plainly meant to sting and insult Steelkilt as though Radney had spat in his face. Any man who has been a sailor on a whale-ship will understand this. And all this, and doubtless much more, the Lakeman fully understood when the mate gave his command. But as he sat still for a moment, and as he steadily looked into the mate's malicious eye, he felt certain that the mate was deliberately provoking him to strike first, so as to have an excuse for beating him. Steelkilt knew well that the mate might lawfully do that. But while thinking all this, he slowly and deliberately swallowed his anger, though it was not easy to do so."

"Therefore, in his ordinary tone, only a little broken by the physical exhaustion he was temporarily in, he answered saying that sweeping the deck was not his business, and he would not do it. And then, without mentioning the shovel at all, he pointed to three lads as the customary sweepers, who, not being assigned to the pumps, had done little or nothing all day. To this, Radney replied with a curse, demanding instant obedience."

"Heated and irritated as he was by his convulsive labor at the pumps, for all his initial nameless impulse to hold back, the sweating Steelkilt could barely stand this behavior from the mate. But somehow still smothering the fire within him, without speaking he remained stubbornly rooted to his seat, until at last the enraged Radney shook the hammer within a few inches of his face, furiously commanding him to obey."

"Steelkilt rose, and slowly retreating around the windlass, steadily followed by the mate with his threatening hammer, deliberately repeated his refusal to obey. Seeing, however, that his restraint had not the slightest effect, by a terrible and unmistakable gesture with his twisted hand he warned off the foolish and obsessed man. But it was no use. And in this way the two went once slowly around the windlass. Then Steelkilt, quickly drawing up a heavy plank from its place, spoke these words:"

"'Mr. Radney, I will not obey you. Take that hammer away, or look to yourself.' But the doomed mate coming still closer to him, where the Lakeman stood fixed, now shook the heavy hammer within an inch of his teeth, meanwhile repeating a string of unbearable curses. Retreating not the thousandth part of an inch, stabbing him in the eye with the unflinching dagger of his glare, Steelkilt, gripping his plank tighter, made a fierce warning beneath his breath — a whisper that sounded as deadly as the click of a cocked pistol. But the mate was already raging beyond reason. The Lakeman's face spoke a command. But the mate would not obey. With one blow of the plank, Steelkilt knocked him flat on the deck, then immediately ran to the rigging."
"Before the cry could reach the stern, Steelkilt was shaking one of the backstays leading far aloft to where two of his comrades were standing their mastheads. They were both Canallers."
"'Canallers!' cried Don Pedro. 'We have seen many whale-ships in our harbors, but never heard of your Canallers. Pardon — who and what are they?'"
"'Canallers, Don, are the boatmen of our great Erie Canal. You must have heard of it.'"
"'No, Senor. Hereabouts in this dull, warm, most lazy, and hereditary land, we know but little of your vigorous North.'"
"'Is that so? Well then, Don, refill my cup. Your chicha is very fine. And before going further I will tell you what our Canallers are, for such information may shed light on my story.'"

"For three hundred and sixty miles, gentlemen, through the entire breadth of the state of New York — through numerous populous cities and thriving villages, through long, dismal, uninhabited swamps and rich cultivated fields unrivaled for fertility — by billiard-room and bar-room, through the sacred heart of great forests, on Roman arches over Indian rivers — through sun and shade, by happy hearts or broken, through all the wide contrasting scenery of those noble Northern states — winds the long Erie Canal. If it were possible for miles, the canal stretches on as straight as a pike. And every mile of it is flanked by side-stretches of the most fertile, most prosperous farm land in the Republic. The vast wealth and beauty of this great canal country gives it an almost European grandeur of appearance."
"'Is that a friar passing?' said Don Pedro, looking down into the crowded plaza with humorous concern."
"'Well for our northern friend that Dame Isabella's Inquisition is waning in Lima,' laughed Don Sebastian. 'Proceed, Senor.'"

"'A moment! Pardon!' cried another of the company. 'In the name of all us Limenos, I merely wish to say to you, sir sailor, that we have by no means overlooked your tact in not substituting present-day Lima for distant Venice in your unflattering comparison. Oh! Do not bow and look surprised — you know the proverb all along this coast: "Corrupt as Lima." It only confirms your point — churches more plentiful than billiard-rooms, and forever open — and "Corrupt as Lima." So too, Venice. I have been there. The holy city of the blessed evangelist, St. Mark! — St. Dominic, purge it! Your cup! Thanks — here I refill. Now, Senor, proceed with your story.'"

"Freely described in his own element, gentlemen, the Canaller would make a fine dramatic hero, so abundantly and colorfully wicked is he. Like Mark Antony, for days upon days along his green-turfed, flowery Nile, he lazily floats, openly enjoying himself, ripening in the sun on the deck. But ashore, all this ease is shed. The piratical look he picked up from the wild sailors he used to associate with in the Atlantic and the lawless freshwater settlements along the canal — all this tells its story. Though now a canal man, there is in him the spirit of something fiercer. He has fought river duels. He has hunted buffalo with the best of them on the plains. He has danced at the Navajos' bonfire. He may have shown himself a tough customer in the riots of the Five Points. And in the hands of the police, has sometimes been carried in a blanket like a baby, when they could get no stretcher. He has told many a straight truth in an odd way that would make a landsman stare. With the face of a desperado and the heart of a lion, he might have been a good many things in this world — if only the world would let him."

"'I see! I see!' exclaimed Don Pedro eagerly, spilling his chicha on his silver ruffles. 'No need to travel! The world's one Lima. I had thought, now, that in your temperate North the generations were cold and holy as the hills. — But the story.'"

"I left off, gentlemen, where the Lakeman shook the backstay. Hardly had he done so when he was surrounded by the three junior mates and the four harpooners, who all crowded him to the deck. But sliding down the ropes like baleful comets, the two Canallers rushed into the uproar and tried to drag their man out of it toward the forecastle. Others of the sailors joined them in this attempt, and a fierce scuffle resulted, in which the officers were eventually victorious. Steelkilt and his desperadoes were locked below. But this did not end the scene. The sailors in the forecastle had a rumor among them that the mate was purposely driving Steelkilt into a fight in order to get a reason to discipline him — all for the purpose of humiliating a man who had made him feel inferior. And when the mates came among them to get volunteers for manning the pumps — for the leak was now growing dangerous — none would volunteer, and the officers had to pump with their own hands. Even this did not shake the crew's stubbornness."
"'Come out of that, you pirates!' roared the captain, now threatening them with a pistol in each hand, just brought to him by the steward. 'Come out of that, you cutthroats!'"

"Steelkilt leaped on the barricade, and striding up and down there, defied the worst the pistols could do. But he gave the captain to understand clearly that his — Steelkilt's — death would be the signal for a murderous mutiny from all hands. Fearing in his heart that this might prove all too true, the captain backed off a little, but still commanded the rebels to return immediately to their duty."
"'Will you promise not to touch us if we do?' demanded their ringleader."
"'Turn to! Turn to! — I make no promise — to your duty! Do you want to sink the ship by knocking off at a time like this? Turn to!' And he once more raised a pistol."

"'Sink the ship?' cried Steelkilt. 'Aye, let her sink. Not a man of us turns to unless you swear not to raise a rope's end against us. What say you, men?' turning to his comrades. A fierce cheer was their response."

"The Lakeman now patrolled the barricade, all the while keeping his eye on the Captain, and throwing out sentences like these: 'It's not our fault. We didn't want it. I told him to take his hammer away. It was a boy's job. He might have known me before this. I told him not to provoke the buffalo. I believe I've broken a finger here against his cursed jaw. Aren't those mincing knives down in the forecastle there, men? Look to those handspikes, my hearties. Captain, by God, look to yourself! Say the word — don't be a fool — forget the flogging — or we're done! Say it! We only asked not to be flogged — that's all. We'll be peaceable — only say the word!'"
"'Turn to! I make no promises. Turn to, I say!'"

"'Look here, now,' cried the Lakeman, flinging out his arm toward him, 'there are a few of us here — and I am one of them — who have shipped for the cruise, do you see? Now as you well know, sir, we can claim our discharge as soon as the anchor is down. So we don't want a fight. It's not in our interest. We want to be peaceable. We are ready to work, but we won't be flogged.'"
"'Turn to!' roared the Captain."

"Steelkilt glanced around him a moment, and then said: 'I tell you what it is now, Captain — rather than kill you, and be hanged for such a shabby rascal, we won't lift a hand against you unless you attack us. But until you give us the word about not flogging us, we don't do a hand's turn.'"
"'Down into the forecastle, then. Down with you! I'll keep you there till you're sick of it. Down you go.'"

"'Shall we?' cried the ringleader to his men. Most of them were against it. But at length, in obedience to Steelkilt, they preceded him down into their dark den, disappearing with growls, like bears into a cave."

"As the Lakeman's bare head was just level with the planks, the Captain and his men leaped the barricade, and rapidly drawing the cover of the hatch shut, planted their group of hands upon it and loudly called for the steward to bring the heavy brass padlock belonging to the companionway. Then opening the hatch a crack, the Captain whispered something down into the dark, closed it, and turned the key."

"All night a wide-awake watch was kept by all the officers, fore and aft, especially about the forecastle hatch and the forward hatchway, where it was feared the rebels might emerge after breaking through the bulkhead below. But the hours of darkness passed in peace. The men who still remained at their duty toiled hard at the pumps, whose clinking and clanking at intervals pierced the dark night like a troubled conscience."

"At sunrise the Captain went forward, and knocking on the deck, summoned the prisoners to work; but with a yell they refused. Water was then lowered down to them, and a couple of handfuls of biscuit were tossed after it; when again turning the key upon them and pocketing it, the Captain returned to the quarter-deck. Twice every day for three days this was repeated; but on the fourth morning a confused wrangling, and then a scuffling was heard, as the customary summons was delivered; and suddenly four men burst up from the forecastle, saying they were ready to turn to. The fetid closeness of the air, and a famishing diet, united perhaps to some fears of ultimate retribution, had constrained them to surrender at discretion. Emboldened by this, the Captain reiterated his demand to the rest, but Steelkilt shouted up to him a terrific hint to stop his babbling and betake himself where he belonged. On the fifth morning three others of the mutineers bolted up into the air from the desperate arms below that sought to restrain them. Only three were left."
"'Better turn to, now?' said the Captain with a heartless jeer."
"'Shut us up again, will you!' cried Steelkilt."
"'Oh certainly,' said the Captain, and the key clicked."

"It was at this point, gentlemen, that enraged by the defection of seven of his former associates, and stung by the mocking voice that had last hailed him, and maddened by his long entombment in a place as black as the bowels of despair — it was then that Steelkilt proposed to the two Canallers, thus far apparently of one mind with him, to burst out of their hole at the next summoning of the garrison; and armed with their keen mincing knives (long, crescentic, heavy implements with a handle at each end), run amok from the bowsprit to the taffrail; and if by any devilishness of desperation possible, seize the ship. For himself, he would do this, he said, whether they joined him or not. That was the last night he should spend in that den. But the scheme met with no opposition on the part of the other two; they swore they were ready for that, or for any other mad thing — for anything, in short, but a surrender. And what was more, they each insisted upon being the first man on deck, when the time to make the rush should come. But to this their leader as fiercely objected, reserving that priority for himself; particularly as his two comrades would not yield, the one to the other, in the matter; and both of them could not be first, for the ladder would but admit one man at a time. And here, gentlemen, the foul play of these miscreants must come out."

"Upon hearing the frantic plan of their leader, each in his own separate soul had suddenly hit upon the same piece of treachery: namely, to be the first to break out so as to be the first of the three — though the last of the ten — to surrender, and thereby secure whatever small chance of pardon such behavior might earn. But when Steelkilt revealed his determination to stay and fight until the last, something changed in their faces. And while he was explaining the details to them — taking them into his full confidence — they suddenly fell upon him, and tied him hand and foot, gagging him with ropes. Then calling to the captain, they demanded release, saying they would now cooperate."

"Thinking murder was at hand and smelling in the dark for blood, the captain and all his armed mates and harpooners rushed for the forecastle. In a few minutes the hatch was opened, and bound hand and foot, the still-struggling ringleader was shoved up into the air by his treacherous allies, who at once claimed the honor of securing a man who had been fully ripe for murder. But all of them were collared and dragged along the deck like dead cattle. And the Captain, at the head of his officers, stood over the three prisoners, with a mixture of relief and contempt."

"At sunrise he summoned all hands, and separating those who had rebelled from those who had taken no part in the mutiny, he told the former that he had a good mind to flog them all round — thought, upon the whole, he would do so — he ought to — justice demanded it. But for the present, considering their timely surrender, he would let them go with a reprimand, which he then delivered in the most violent terms."

"'But as for you, you carrion rogues,' turning to the three men in the rigging — 'for you, I mean to mince you up for the try-pots.' And seizing a rope, he applied it with all his might to the backs of the two traitors, until they yelled no more, but lifelessly hung their heads sideways, like the two crucified thieves are drawn."

"'My wrist is sprained with you!' he cried at last. 'But there is still rope enough left for you, my fine bantam, who wouldn't give up. Take that gag from his mouth, and let us hear what he can say for himself.'"

"For a moment the exhausted mutineer made a trembling motion of his cramped jaws, and then painfully twisting his head around, said in a sort of hiss, 'What I say is this — and mind it well — if you flog me, I murder you!'"
"'Say you so? Then see how you frighten me' — and the Captain drew back with the rope to strike."
"'Best not,' hissed the Lakeman."
"'But I must' — and the rope was once more drawn back for the stroke."

"Steelkilt here hissed out something inaudible to all but the Captain, who, to the amazement of all hands, started back, paced the deck rapidly two or three times, and then suddenly throwing down his rope, said, 'I won't do it — let him go — cut him down, do you hear?'"

"But as the junior mates were hurrying to carry out the order, a pale man with a bandaged head stopped them — Radney, the chief mate. Ever since the blow, he had lain in his berth. But that morning, hearing the commotion on deck, he had crept out, and thus far had watched the whole scene. His mouth was in such a state that he could hardly speak. But mumbling something about being willing and able to carry out the Captain's sentence himself, he snatched the rope from the Captain's relaxed hands — in that instant, by turns maddened with pain and revenge — and advancing toward the strung-up man, ignoring Steelkilt's warning, he dealt the blow."
"'You are a coward!' hissed the Lakeman."

"'So I am, but take that.' The mate was in the very act of striking when another hiss stayed his raised arm. He paused — and then pausing no more, made good on his word, in spite of Steelkilt's threat, whatever that might have been. The three men were then cut down, all hands were turned to, and sullenly worked by the moody seamen, the iron pumps clanged as before."

"Just after dark that day, when one watch had gone below, a commotion was heard in the forecastle. The two trembling traitors came running up and besieged the cabin door, saying they dared not stay with the crew. Pleas, cuffs, and kicks could not drive them back. So at their own request they were locked down in the ship's hold for safety. Still, no sign of mutiny reappeared among the rest. On the contrary, the seamen carried out all their duties in a quiet, obedient fashion. And Steelkilt obeyed his orders, and so did all the rest of those who had been in the forecastle. As to whether the Captain quietly put away his pistols, I do not know. But I heard later that Steelkilt whispered to them all a strategy of some kind. The crew then showed a strange respect toward the mate, who grew more and more pleasant and even sociable toward them. Even Steelkilt's savage face appeared to be softening, and the Lakeman showed signs of wanting to let bygones be bygones."

"But though the Lakeman had persuaded the seamen to adopt this sort of passivity in their conduct, he kept his own counsel — at least until all was over — concerning his own proper and private revenge upon the man who had stung him in the deepest part of his heart. He was in Radney the chief mate's watch. And as if the doomed man sought to run more than halfway to meet his fate, after the scene at the forecastle he continued to push Steelkilt in small, persistent ways."

"During the night, Radney had an unseamanlike habit of sitting on the bulwarks of the quarterdeck and leaning his arm upon the gunwale of the boat that was hoisted up there, a little above the ship's side. In this position, it was well known, he sometimes dozed. There was a considerable gap between the boat and the ship, and down between them was the sea. Steelkilt calculated his time, and found that his next watch below would come at two in the morning of the third night after the flogging. He went to his hammock and looked for something. It was a piece of cord and a ball of iron — the makings of a slungshot."
"'What are you making there?' said a shipmate."
"'What do you think? What does it look like?'"
"'Like a lanyard for your bag. But it's an odd one, seems to me.'"
"'Yes, rather odd,' said the Lakeman, holding it at arm's length before him. 'But I think it will do. Shipmate, I haven't enough twine — have you any?'"
"But there was none in the forecastle."
"'Then I must get some from old Rad.' And he rose to go aft."
"'You don't mean to go begging to him!' said a sailor."

"'Why not? Do you think he won't do me a turn, when it's to help himself in the end, shipmate?' And going to the mate, he looked at him quietly and asked him for some twine to mend his hammock. It was given him — neither twine nor slungshot were seen again. But the next night an iron ball, closely netted, partly rolled from the pocket of the Lakeman's jacket as he was tucking the coat into his hammock for a pillow. Twenty-four hours later, Steelkilt and his mates would have been at work. But at this point, gentlemen, a fool saved the would-be murderer from the bloody deed he had planned."

"But, gentlemen, a fool saved the would-be murderer from the bloody deed he had planned. Yet complete revenge he had, and without being the avenger. For by a mysterious fate, Heaven itself seemed to step in to take out of his hands into its own the damning thing he would have done."

"It was just between daybreak and sunrise on the morning of the second day, when they were washing down the decks, that a stupid Tenerife man, drawing water in the main-chains, all at once shouted out, 'There she rolls! There she rolls!' Jesus, what a whale! It was Moby Dick."
"'Moby Dick!' cried Don Sebastian. 'St. Dominic! Sir sailor, but do whales have christenings? Whom do you call Moby Dick?'"
"'A very white, and famous, and most deadly immortal monster, Don — but that would be too long a story.'"
"'How? How?' cried all the young Spaniards, crowding around."
"'No, Dons, Dons — no, no! I cannot tell that now. Let me get more into the air, Sirs.'"
"'The chicha! The chicha!' cried Don Pedro. 'Our vigorous friend looks faint — fill up his empty glass!'"

"No need, gentlemen; one moment, and I proceed. — Now, gentlemen, so suddenly perceiving the snowy whale within fifty yards of the ship — forgetful of the compact among the crew — in the excitement of the moment, the Teneriffe man had instinctively and involuntarily lifted his voice for the monster, though for some little time past it had been plainly beheld from the three sullen mast-heads. All was now a frenzy. 'The White Whale — the White Whale!' was the cry from captain, mates, and harpooneers, who, undeterred by fearful rumors, were all anxious to capture so famous and precious a fish; while the dogged crew eyed askance, and with curses, the appalling beauty of the vast milky mass, that, lit up by a horizontal spangling sun, shifted and glistened like a living opal in the blue morning sea. Gentlemen, a strange fatality pervades the whole career of these events, as if verily mapped out before the world itself was charted. The mutineer was the bowsman of the mate, and when fast to a fish, it was his duty to sit next him, while Radney stood up with his lance in the prow, and haul in or slacken the line, at the word of command. Moreover, when the four boats were lowered, the mate's got the start; and none howled more fiercely with delight than did Steelkilt, as he strained at his oar. After a stiff pull, their harpooneer got fast, and, spear in hand, Radney sprang to the bow. He was always a furious man, it seems, in a boat. And now his bandaged cry was, to beach him on the whale's topmost back. Nothing loath, his bowsman hauled him up and up, through a blinding foam that blent two whitenesses together, till of a sudden the boat struck as against a sunken ledge, and, keeling over, spilled out the standing mate. That instant, as he fell on the whale's slippery back, the boat righted, and was dashed aside by the swell, while Radney was tossed over into the sea, on the other flank of the whale. He struck out through the spray, and, for an instant, was dimly seen through that veil, wildly seeking to remove himself from the eye of Moby Dick. But the whale rushed round in a sudden maelstrom, seized the swimmer between his jaws, and rearing high up with him, plunged headlong again, and went down."

"Meanwhile, at the first bump of the boat's bottom, the Lakeman had slackened the line so as to drop back from the whirlpool. Calmly looking on, he thought his own thoughts. But a sudden, terrific, downward jerk of the boat quickly brought his knife to the line. He cut it, and the whale was free. But at some distance, Moby Dick rose again, with some tatters of Radney's red woolen shirt caught in the teeth that had destroyed him. The four remaining boats came up to the rescue, but the whale fled, and the sailor was gone."

"In good time, the Town-Ho reached her port — a savage, solitary place where no civilized creature lived. There, led by the Lakeman, all but five or six of the forecastle men deliberately deserted among the palms. Eventually, as it turned out, they seized a large double war-canoe of the natives and set sail for some other harbor."

"The ship's company being reduced to but a handful, the captain called upon the Islanders to assist him in the laborious business of heaving down the ship to stop the leak. But to such unresting vigilance over their dangerous allies was this small band of whites necessitated, both by night and by day, and so extreme was the hard work they underwent, that upon the vessel being ready again for sea, they were in such a weakened condition that the captain durst not put off with them in so heavy a vessel. After taking counsel with his officers, he anchored the ship as far off shore as possible, loaded and ran out his two cannon from the bows, stacked his muskets on the poop, and warning the Islanders not to approach the ship at their peril, took one man with him, and setting the sail of his best whale-boat, steered straight before the wind for Tahiti, five hundred miles distant, to procure a reinforcement to his crew."

"On the fourth day of the sail, a large canoe was spotted, which seemed to have stopped at a low coral island. He steered away from it. But the savage craft bore down on him, and soon the voice of Steelkilt hailed him to heave to, or he would run him under water. The captain presented a pistol. With one foot on each prow of the yoked war-canoes, the Lakeman laughed him to scorn, assuring him that if the pistol was fired, he would immediately be sunk — the canoe being much faster than the whale-boat. He repeated his demand."
"'What do you want of me?' cried the captain."
"'Where are you bound? And for what are you bound?' demanded Steelkilt. 'No lies.'"
"'I am bound to Tahiti for more men.'"
"'Very good. Let me board you a moment — I come in peace.' With that he leaped from the canoe, swam to the boat, and climbing the gunwale, stood face to face with the captain."

"'Cross your arms, sir. Throw back your head. Now, repeat after me. As soon as Steelkilt leaves me, I swear to beach this boat on that island and remain there six days. If I do not, may lightning strike me!'"
"'A pretty scholar,' laughed the Lakeman. 'Adios, Senor!' And leaping into the sea, he swam back to his comrades."

"Watching the boat until it was fairly beached and drawn up to the roots of the coconut trees, Steelkilt set sail again, and in due time arrived at Tahiti, his own destination. There luck befriended him. Two ships were about to sail for France and were providentially in need of precisely that number of men which the sailor led. They embarked, and so forever got the start of their former captain, had he been at all disposed to pursue them."

"Some ten days after the French ships sailed, the whale-boat arrived, and the captain was forced to enlist some of the more civilized Tahitians, who had been somewhat used to the sea. Chartering a small native schooner, he returned with them to his vessel, and finding all well there, again resumed his cruising."

"Where Steelkilt now is, gentlemen, no one knows. But upon the island of Nantucket, the widow of Radney still turns to the sea which refuses to give up its dead — still in dreams sees the awful white whale that destroyed him."
"'Are you through?' said Don Sebastian quietly."
"'I am, Don.'"

"'Then I beg you, tell me if to the best of your own convictions, this story of yours is in substance really true? It is so passing wonderful! Did you get it from an unquestionable source? Bear with me if I seem to press.'"
"'Also bear with all of us, sir sailor, for we all join in Don Sebastian's request,' cried the company, with great interest."
"'Is there a copy of the Holy Gospels in the Golden Inn, gentlemen?'"
"'No,' said Don Sebastian, 'but I know a worthy priest nearby who will quickly get one for me. I go for it — but are you sure about this? This may grow too serious.'"
"'Will you be so good as to bring the priest also, Don?'"

"'Though there are no burnings at the stake in Lima now,' said one of the company to another, 'I fear our sailor friend risks the attention of the archbishop. Let us move further out of the moonlight. I see no need for this.'"
"'Excuse me for running after you, Don Sebastian — but may I also ask that you will be particular in getting the largest-sized Gospels you can.'"
"'This is the priest. He brings you the Gospels,' said Don Sebastian, gravely, returning with a tall and solemn figure."
"'Let me remove my hat. Now, venerable priest, further into the light, and hold the Holy Book before me that I may touch it."

"'So help me Heaven, and on my honor the story I have told you, gentlemen, is in substance and its great items, true. I know it to be true. It happened on this earth. I walked that ship. I knew the crew. I have seen and talked with Steelkilt since the death of Radney.'"
